title: Probability

notes.heading: 1. Axioms, Addition Theorem & De Morgan Event Algebra
notes.proseLatex: On a sample space $S$, probability satisfies $0 \le P(A) \le 1$, $P(S)=1$, and $P(\bar{A}) = 1 - P(A)$. For any two events, $P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)$; mutually exclusive (disjoint) events have $A\cap B = \emptyset \implies P(A\cap B) = 0$. De Morgan's laws $P(\bar{A}\cap\bar{B}) = P(\overline{A\cup B}) = 1 - P(A\cup B)$ convert 'neither $A$ nor $B$' into union complements.

keyFormulas.label: Addition Law & De Morgan Complement
keyFormulas.latex: $P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B),\qquad P(\bar{A}\cap\bar{B}) = 1 - P(A\cup B)$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Translate verbal event statements into union, intersection and complement.

examples.problemLatex: If $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$, and $A, B$ are independent, find $P(\bar{A}\cap\bar{B})$.
stepsLatex: Independence gives $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.20$, so $P(A\cup B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.20 = 0.70$.

notes.heading: 2. Conditional Probability, Independence & Bayes' Theorem
notes.proseLatex: For $P(B) > 0$, conditional probability is $P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$. Events $A, B$ are statistically independent if and only if $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, which also implies $\bar{A}, \bar{B}$ are independent and $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\bar{A})P(\bar{B})$. Given a partition $E_1,\dots,E_k$ of $S$, total probability is $P(A) = \sum_i P(E_i)P(A\mid E_i)$ and Bayes' theorem reverses conditioning to give posterior $P(E_j\mid A)$.

keyFormulas.label: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem
keyFormulas.latex: $P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(E_j\mid A) = \frac{P(E_j)\,P(A\mid E_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} P(E_i)\,P(A\mid E_i)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Apply total probability and Bayes' theorem to two-bag or defective-item problems.

examples.problemLatex: Machine $M_1$ makes $60\%$ of bolts ($2\%$ defective) and $M_2$ makes $40\%$ ($5\%$ defective). Given a bolt is defective, find $P(M_2\mid D)$.

notes.heading: 3. Binomial Trials, Mean & Variance
notes.proseLatex: In $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability $p$ and failure $q = 1-p$, the number of successes $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$ has PMF $P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r}p^r q^{n-r}$ for $r = 0,1,\dots,n$. Its expectation is $\mu = np$ and variance is $\sigma^2 = npq$, which immediately implies $\sigma^2 < \mu$ for every valid binomial distribution ($0 < q < 1$) — a classic JELET consistency check!

keyFormulas.label: Binomial Distribution PMF, Mean & Variance
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Recover n and p from binomial mean and variance and reject impossible pairs.

wbjeebTraps: Mutually exclusive vs independent trap: for events with $P(A)>0, P(B)>0$, mutually exclusive ($P(A\cap B)=0$) and independent ($P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)>0$) CANNOT both hold!
In binomial distributions, variance $\sigma^2 = npq$ MUST be strictly less than mean $\mu = np$; e.g., mean $= 4$, variance $= 5$ is impossible.
Remember $P(A\mid B) \neq P(B\mid A)$ unless $P(A) = P(B)$.
